title: Prepositions
in30Seconds: Prepositions are relationship words. They sit before a noun phrase and show how it connects to the rest of the sentence: where (in the kitchen, on the counter, at the bus stop), when (in August, on Friday, at six), or which way (to the station, from home, through the tunnel). A preposition plus its object forms a prepositional phrase that modifies like an adjective or adverb. Since preposition choice follows patterns rather than strict rules, fixed combinations are best learned as units.
whyItMatters: Prepositions carry a lot of meaning in very few letters. Choosing the right one changes the picture: a meeting can happen in the library, on the library steps, or at the library, and readers need to know which. Academic and professional writing depends on precise relationships, between evidence and claim, cause and effect, method and result, and prepositions are often the words that mark those links. For multilingual learners, prepositions are a common source of errors not because of any personal weakness but because every language divides space, time, and direction differently; some languages have no prepositions at all. Learning the main patterns, and treating tricky combinations as vocabulary to memorize, turns a frequent source of confusion into a manageable skill that pays off in reading, writing, and everyday communication.
learningObjectives: Define a preposition and explain the kinds of relationships prepositions signal.
Distinguish in, on, and at for both place and time.
Identify direction and movement prepositions such as to, from, into, out of, across, and through.
Identify prepositional phrases and determine whether each modifies like an adjective or like an adverb.
Apply verb + preposition combinations such as depend on, listen to, and rely on.
Evaluate the formal-writing guideline against ending sentences with prepositions and explain its limits.

collegeVersion.heading: Relationship words with a small word count
collegeVersion.body: A preposition is a word that typically appears before a noun phrase and shows how that phrase relates to the rest of the sentence. The relationship can be spatial: the keys are in the drawer, the poster is on the wall, the courier is at the gate. It can be temporal: the semester ends in May, the exam is on Tuesday, the class starts at 8:30. It can also be logical: she wrote the report for her supervisor, the grant was funded despite the budget cuts, everyone agreed with the proposal. English has more than one hundred common prepositions, and many are very short words, easy to overlook yet able to change the whole picture of a sentence when chosen wrong. Some prepositions span several words, such as out of or because of, but they act as a single unit. A useful reading habit is to pause at each preposition and ask what relationship it names.

collegeVersion.heading: In, on, and at: the classic place and time patterns
collegeVersion.body: The most practical trio is in, on, and at. For place, think about geometry. At treats a location as a point or exact position: you wait at the bus stop or live at a specific address such as 15 Craig Street. On treats a location as a surface: the mail sits on the counter, the picture hangs on the wall, the city of London lies on the River Thames. In treats a location as an enclosed space or area: the milk is in the fridge, the children play in the park, English layers habits on top of that geometry: you ride on a bus or plane but in a car or taxi, and you are at work or at school, places tied to activities. For time, the same three words divide differently. At goes with clock times and particular moments: at noon, at midnight, at 8:30. On goes with days and dates: on Friday, on New Year's Day, on 19 October. In goes with longer periods: months, years, seasons, and parts of the day, as in in December or in 2026. The two systems share the same words but organize them differently, so it helps to practice place and time as separate patterns.

collegeVersion.heading: Direction and movement: to, from, into, out of, across, through
collegeVersion.body: When the relationship involves motion, English uses a separate set of prepositions. To marks movement toward a destination: the ferry sails to the island. From marks the starting point: the flight leaves from gate 12. Into signals movement toward the interior of a space: the water poured into the tank. Out of signals movement from inside to outside: the cat slipped out of the carrier. Across signals movement to the other side of a surface or line: we walked across the bridge. Through signals movement from one side of a space to the other, with the space surrounding the path: the train rumbled through the tunnel. Direction prepositions appear with verbs of motion; location prepositions appear with state verbs such as be. Compare the ball is in the box with the ball rolled into the box: the first describes where the ball sits, the second describes where it moves. Noticing this contrast helps with pairs such as in and into, or on and onto.

collegeVersion.heading: Prepositional phrases as modifiers
collegeVersion.body: A preposition does not stand alone; it opens a phrase. A prepositional phrase consists of the preposition plus its object, most often a noun phrase, and the whole phrase works as a modifier, like an adjective or an adverb. In the sentence the waiter set the plates on the table by the window, the phrase on the table modifies the verb set, telling where the action happened, while by the window modifies the noun table, telling which table. The same phrase can attach to different targets in different sentences, so the useful habit is to ask: what word is this phrase adding detail to? When a prepositional phrase modifies a noun, it narrows the noun, like an adjective; when it modifies a verb, it adds information about place, time, or manner, like an adverb. Because prepositional phrases can pile up, writers keep each one close to the word it modifies: in the report on the desk in the office near the elevator, each phrase attaches to the noun before it, and moving one quietly changes the meaning.

collegeVersion.heading: Verb + preposition combinations and the mistakes to expect
collegeVersion.body: Some verbs attract a particular preposition, and the pair functions as a unit: the grade depends on the project, the committee listens to the testimony, the student relies on the study guide, the guests wait for the bus. There is no general rule predicting which preposition follows which verb, so learners memorize the verb with its preposition inside a full phrase. Because preposition systems differ across languages, a learner whose first language organizes space and time differently will predictably reach for a different preposition at first; that is an expected step, not a failure. Formal writing often avoids ending a sentence with a preposition, preferring the tool with which we work over the tool we work with. The objection, however, is a stylistic convention with a documented seventeenth-century origin, not a rule of grammar; everyday speech and most informal writing place prepositions at the end comfortably. The practical move is to match the register: rephrase in formal academic writing when the alternative reads naturally, and otherwise keep natural word order. Note that phrasal verbs, where a verb plus a particle changes meaning as a unit, belong to the verbs topic; this lesson covers prepositions themselves and their phrases.

vocabulary.definition: A word that appears before a noun phrase and shows a relationship such as place, time, direction, or logical connection.
A group of words made of a preposition plus its object; the phrase modifies other words the way adjectives and adverbs do.
The noun phrase or other unit that follows the preposition and completes the phrase, such as the drawer in in the drawer.
A word or phrase that adds detail to another word, such as a prepositional phrase adding where or when information.
A pair of words that regularly appear together, such as depend on; the combination is learned as a unit rather than chosen by rule.
A group of words that works as a single preposition, such as out of, in front of, or because of.
The placement of a preposition at the end of a clause or sentence; normal in everyday English, often avoided in formal writing.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Prepositions are the small words that place things in relation to other things. Think of a sentence as a photograph: the nouns are the people and objects in the frame, the verbs are the action, and the prepositions decide where everything stands. The cat is in the box, on the box, near the box, or behind the box, and each preposition takes a different picture. The same idea works for time: the meeting is in June, on the third, at ten. It even works for abstract ideas: you agree with a person, apologize for a mistake, and depend on a plan. There is no master rule that tells you which preposition to use with every word, so the practical move is to learn the big patterns, especially in, on, and at for place and time, and to memorize the fixed pairs that come up again and again. When you read, notice how often the little words carry the real relationship. When you write, check that each one points where you mean it to point.
eli10.analogy: Think of prepositions as labels on a shelf. In means the object goes inside the shelf; on means it rests on top of the shelf; at means it stands at the exact spot where the shelf meets the wall. When you pack a bag, you put clothes in the bag, set the book on the bag, and wait at the door; each word draws a different picture of where things are. The labels work for time too: in the week that is coming, on the day you circle on the calendar, at the hour the clock shows.
eli10.analogyLimits: The shelf picture only goes so far. Many prepositions express relationships that have nothing to do with physical position, such as for in waiting for a bus or of in afraid of heights. And English habits sometimes ignore geometry: you sit on a bus but in a car. So treat the spatial picture as a helpful start, not a guarantee, and learn fixed combinations as vocabulary.

workedExample: Imagine you are writing directions for a friend who is meeting you before a concert. You text: Meet me at the south entrance on Friday at 6:15. Walk in through the main doors, then look for the ticket booth on your left, across from the souvenir stand. The band usually waits behind the stage curtain, so arrive early. Every preposition does a job here: at marks the exact entrance, on and at handle the day and the time, through describes moving inside, for follows the verb look, on and across describe position in the lobby, and behind places the band relative to the curtain. Change one preposition, from meet me at the south entrance to meet me in the south entrance or the booth on the right, and the picture changes. Noticing these choices in your own sentences is the fastest way to control them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a preposition by translating it word-for-word from another language, as in depending of the weather when the learner's first language uses one word where English uses several.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat preposition choice as language-specific: memorize fixed combinations such as depend on, listen to, and rely on with their verbs, and expect to relearn some pairings as you go.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using in, on, and at interchangeably for place, as in the coffee mugs are in the top shelf or we waited on the museum entrance.
commonMistakes.correction: Use at for points and exact positions, on for surfaces, and in for enclosed spaces: mugs belong on a shelf, and you wait at an entrance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a sentence-final preposition as always wrong and twisting the sentence to avoid it, which can produce stiff phrasing.
commonMistakes.correction: Sentence-final prepositions are normal in English; the avoidance guideline is a formal-style preference with a seventeenth-century origin. In formal academic writing, rephrase when the alternative reads naturally, but do not treat the guideline as a grammar error in speech or everyday writing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the same preposition for every type of transport, as in she rode in the bus to school.
commonMistakes.correction: English uses on for buses, trains, planes, and ships, but in for cars and taxis: she rode on the bus, yet she drove in her car.

compareContrast.distinction: For place, in marks an enclosed space or area, on marks a surface, and at marks a point or exact position; the same three words follow different rules for time, so place and time should be practiced separately.
A word such as before works as a preposition when it is followed by a noun phrase (before the meeting) and as a conjunction when it is followed by a clause (before the meeting began).
A prepositional phrase can modify a noun, as in the book on the shelf (which book?), or modify a verb, as in she placed it on the shelf (where?); the target word decides the role.

A prepositional phrase is a modifier built from a preposition plus a noun phrase; a phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle or preposition whose meaning changes as a unit, such as turn off or catch up, and it gets full treatment in the verbs lesson.

keyTakeaway: Prepositions are small relationship words with a big job: learn the in, on, and at patterns for place and time, memorize verb + preposition combinations as units, and let the register decide how formal your preposition use needs to be.

questionBank.prompt: What is the main job of a preposition in a sentence?
options: It shows a relationship, often of place, time, or direction, between words in a sentence.
It names a person, place, thing, or idea.
It expresses an action, occurrence, or state.
It connects two clauses of equal grammatical weight.
questionBank.explanation: A preposition links its object to the rest of the sentence, showing relationships such as place, time, or direction; naming is a noun's job, action belongs to verbs, and equal-weight connectors are coordinating conjunctions.
questionBank.skill: recognizing the grammatical function of prepositions

questionBank.prompt: Which sentence uses the place preposition correctly?
options: The coffee mugs are in the top shelf of the cabinet.
We waited on the museum's main entrance for half an hour.
She left her phone on the kitchen counter.
The children swam on the hotel pool all morning.
questionBank.explanation: A shelf is a surface, so the mugs belong on it, not in it; an entrance is treated as a point, so you wait at it; and a pool is an enclosed space, so swimmers are in it. Only the counter sentence is right, because a counter is a surface and on marks surfaces.
questionBank.skill: applying the in, on, and at distinction for place

questionBank.prompt: Which sentence uses the time preposition correctly?
options: The workshop begins on 9:00 a.m.
My cousin was born at 1998.
We have choir practice in Tuesdays.
The library closes at midnight.
questionBank.explanation: Clock times take at, days take on, and months and years take in. On 9:00 a.m. and in Tuesdays reverse those patterns, and a year takes in, not at; at midnight is correct because midnight is a specific clock moment.
questionBank.skill: choosing at, in, or on for time expressions

questionBank.prompt: In the sentence 'The waiter set the plates on the table by the window,' which prepositional phrase modifies a noun, and which noun does it modify?
options: 'on the table' — it modifies the noun 'plates'
'by the window' — it modifies the noun 'table'
'the waiter set' — it modifies the verb 'set'
'the window' — it modifies the noun 'table'
questionBank.explanation: By the window is a prepositional phrase acting like an adjective: it tells which table. On the table is also a prepositional phrase, but it acts like an adverb by telling where the waiter set the plates, so that option mislabels its role; the remaining options are not prepositional phrases.
questionBank.skill: identifying prepositional phrases and their modifying role

questionBank.prompt: Which preposition correctly completes this sentence? 'The final grade depends ______ the project report, not the in-class quiz.'
options: of
on
for
with
questionBank.explanation: Depend on is a fixed verb + preposition combination, so on is the only option that completes the pattern; of, for, and with do not combine with depend in this meaning, and combinations like this are learned as units rather than chosen by rule.
